name: Research Ethics Conventions
description: This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on research ethics so output stays consistent and easy to review.
content:
This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on research ethics so output stays consistent and easy to review.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Validate research ethics outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
2. When multiple research ethics strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
3. Prefer the simplest research ethics approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
4. When research ethics guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
5. Document any non-obvious research ethics decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
6. Surface known limitations of a chosen research ethics approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
7. Keep research ethics outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
8. When research ethics decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
9. Re-check edge cases relevant to research ethics (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
10. Measure before optimizing any research ethics bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated research ethics concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting research ethics assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of research ethics correctness.
- Do not apply generic research ethics advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for research ethics, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
